statement: The game shall provide players with a smooth and enjoyable puzzle experience.
The game shall remain interesting for adults.
Players shall be able to understand their progress clearly.
Players shall be encouraged to replay the game or improve their times and scores.
The game shall be a solid standalone game that people enjoy using and returning to.
Players are a key stakeholder group for Qheadache.
Game designers or content owners are a key stakeholder group for Qheadache.
An administrator or support person may be needed for Qheadache.
The administrator or support person is responsible for managing the game setup, reviewing progress data, and handling updates and issues.
The administrator shall be able to set up or change the puzzles that are available.
The administrator shall be able to configure the board layout of available puzzles.
The administrator shall be able to configure the predefined challenge that the player has to solve.
The system should support adjusting puzzle difficulty.
The system should support showing different challenges to beginners and to more advanced players.
The administrator should have access to player results records.
The system should allow player results and progress records to be cleared if needed.
Changes should be applied centrally.
Changes should take effect the next time the game starts.
Small setting changes should be applied immediately when it is safe to do so.
The interview should focus on clarifying what the game should do.
The interview should focus on clarifying who the game is for.
The interview should focus on clarifying how progress should be handled.
The interview should focus on clarifying how results should be handled.
The representative can speak to the intended use and business needs behind Qheadache.
The game should support players.
The system should keep information about players' play.
Qheadache shall be designed to be approachable for younger beginners while remaining interesting for adults.
There is no formal system in place for the specific game.
The system shall provide a simple way to restart or try the puzzle again.
The system shall provide basic feedback when a player solves the puzzle.
Additional features should be considered later to determine whether they are worth adding.
The board shall support mouse input for moving blocks if possible.
The board shall support touch input for moving blocks if possible.
The system shall make it obvious whether a move is valid.
The invalid-move feedback shall not interrupt play too much.
The system shall preserve a player's current progress so the player can return later and continue from the same point.
The system shall store the completion time after a puzzle is finished.
The system shall store the number of actions after a puzzle is finished.
The system shall store the score after a puzzle is finished.
The system shall automatically save progress and results without requiring any extra action from the player.
The player's result shall reflect the whole attempt.
The system shall let the player start the current puzzle over from the original beginning state.
The reset or replay option shall work quickly during play.
The reset or replay option shall be easy to find during play.
When the player solves the puzzle, the game shall clearly indicate that the puzzle has been completed.
The game shall not use a harsh game-over failure state in the usual sense.
If the game includes a failure condition, it shall be gentle, such as running out of a limit, and shall offer restart or retry options.
If the game does not include a real failure condition, success feedback shall be the main feedback focus.
The system shall support level creation for puzzle designers and game maintainers.
The system shall support difficulty tuning for puzzle designers and game maintainers.
The system shall support saved progress for puzzle designers and game maintainers.
If the system is intended for education or younger users, it shall provide clear progress tracking.
The system shall preserve saved results for distribution and update stakeholders.
The system shall maintain compatibility for distribution and update stakeholders.
The game shall install and run reliably on the intended computer without special setup.
The game should maintain a simple player record or history that remembers past completion times for each puzzle.
The interface should remain very straightforward.
Qheadache shall be a simple standalone puzzle game that players can start solving immediately without needing anything else.
Qheadache shall provide a fun block-moving puzzle experience.
Qheadache shall be suitable for beginners as well as adults.
Qheadache shall provide clear feedback on player performance.
Qheadache shall track player progress and results.
Qheadache shall track time.
Qheadache shall track moves or actions.
Qheadache shall track score.
Qheadache shall let players see their improvement and replay challenges.
The game shall not require ongoing online services.
The main stakeholders are the product owner or sponsor, the small development team, and the person responsible for testing gameplay and usability.
The product owner shall define the puzzle vision.
The product owner shall make the final decision on priority changes during design and development.
Developers shall fix issues as they arise.
The game shall be fun.
The game shall have balanced challenge.
The game logic shall be maintainable.
A game session shall start when the player launches a puzzle.
The system should save progress during play if doing so is safe.
The team should review results and issues after testing or release.
The system shall block invalid moves cleanly.
The system shall fail gracefully when save data is corrupted.
The system shall handle unexpected actions conservatively.
The game shall handle basic invalid actions quietly and consistently.
Mobile support should be treated as out of scope unless the sponsor decides otherwise.
Automatic updates are mostly a distribution concern.
The system shall use a dynamic autosave approach if it can remain invisible to the player.
The system shall keep player notifications during gameplay very subtle if notifications are used.
Invalid moves shall never change the board state.
The system shall support adaptive autosave based on player activity.
The game shall still load cleanly when a player switches between sessions or reopens a game after a long time.
The system shall track the player's session.
The system shall retain history of completed puzzles or attempts.
External integrations are out of scope for the first version of the game.
Potential future integrations may include simple update checks or optional stats export, but this has not been decided.
Stats export should be simple and local.
The game shall be forgiving.
The game shall allow players to undo moves easily without penalty.
The game shall allow players to restart a puzzle easily without penalty.
The game shall provide a subtle hint system for players who are stuck.
The game shall preserve the challenge while preventing mistakes from turning into frustration.
Update prompts shall feel rare and low-pressure.
Update prompts shall appear ideally only after the player finishes a game or returns to a menu.
The stats view shall be simple and display clear numbers.
The system shall provide an export confirmation so the player knows the stats file was created successfully.
The system should provide a dedicated menu option for stats export and progress viewing.
The system should show the player their overall progress in the progress or settings area.
By default, the system should export only basic stats.
If an update check fails, the game shall fail quietly with a simple message indicating that it could not connect.
If an update check fails, the game shall provide an option to try again later.
If stats export fails, the game shall provide the player with a clear explanation in plain language and indicate whether the data was saved elsewhere.
The system shall provide a very simple progress view that shows the basics at a glance.
The progress view shall show puzzles completed.
The progress view shall show the current time on the active puzzle.
The progress view shall show best results if available.
The system shall provide additional progress details behind an extra click when a user wants more detail.
The system shall allow the player to access progress or stats through a menu such as Progress or Stats.
The system shall allow the player to choose what they want to view before exporting.
The system shall offer an optional choice to include detailed session records in the export if that support is implemented.
The game shall not implement heavy-handed security measures such as account security or online protection.
The game shall perform basic integrity checks on saved data so that corrupted save data can be detected.
The game shall keep saved data minimal.
The game shall avoid collecting personal data unless there is a very clear reason to do so.
The game should detect obvious tampering only when it can do so without causing problems for honest players.
If a saved game appears invalid, the game should mark that save as unreliable.
The system should remain lightweight.
The system should handle a fairly large number of puzzle records without slowing down the game.
The system should summarize old session data after a while so the save file does not grow forever.
If storage becomes an issue, the system should warn the player.
The system should use compression for saved data when it helps keep files small.
The system should use a simple indexed structure so it does not have to scan everything every time it opens stats or progress.
The system should support modular loading for the puzzle library so only the needed content is loaded rather than the entire set at once.
The system should avoid techniques that are too complex if they risk reliability.
The game shall automatically summarize older puzzle records when they are no longer needed in full detail.
If the save file gets close to a practical limit, the game shall warn the player and explain what is happening before anything is lost.
The game shall preserve meaningful progress and keep the game responsive.
The game shall not require the player to manage storage manually.
The game should keep saved progress data well below a size that the average local machine would notice.
In normal use, the player should not have to think about disk space.
When the storage limit is approaching, the game should give a gentle warning.
When the storage limit is approaching, the game should not trim or summarize the recent progress the player is most likely to care about.
When the storage limit is exceeded, the game should continue normally.
The system shall never lose recent progress.
The system shall keep the save file small.
The system shall prioritize protecting the player’s current game over keeping the save file small.
The system shall make its behavior predictable.
The system shall not lock in a hard capacity limit number yet, because the appropriate limit depends on the final storage format and the amount of data a typical session produces.
The system shall begin warnings well before the save becomes a problem.
When summarization starts, the system shall apply it first to the oldest detailed history, not to current or recent data.
The game shall present warnings subtly during normal play.
The game shall display a small notification after a save or between puzzles.
The game shall avoid interrupting the game flow when showing normal warnings or notifications.
The game shall use a modal dialog when the situation becomes more serious.
The game shall show a modal dialog only when the player needs to make a decision or acknowledge that older data was condensed.
The game shall not show repeated reminders unless the problem remains unresolved.
The game should primarily target younger beginners, casual players, and adults who enjoy puzzle games.
For beginners, the game should feel easy to understand.
For more experienced or adult players, the game should remain engaging and challenging enough to feel satisfying.
The first release shall include a basic playable puzzle game.
The first release shall include a set of predefined challenges.
Updates shall be handled in a planned way.
The system shall allow new content such as extra puzzles or small gameplay improvements to be added in later versions.
Player feedback about confusing or too difficult features shall be reviewed.
Older saved games should still work after updates.
Starting fresh is acceptable only if a major change makes old saves impossible to use.
Cases where old saves cannot be used should be rare and clearly explained.
The application shall use simple and consistent language.
Records and help text should use the terms "time taken," "number of moves," "score," "current puzzle," and "completed puzzle."
A puzzle is solved when the player reaches the predefined goal state for that challenge.
The system should keep the terms used in menus and help text the same everywhere as much as possible.
The system may allow a different word in a special context if it is clearer.
The game shall run as a self-contained desktop application that users open and play on their own computer without needing any other system.
In normal use, the game shall launch.
The game shall save progress locally on the same machine.
The game shall be easy to start and use in a typical home or school setting without requiring special setup.
The desktop game should run well on ordinary computers without requiring high-end hardware.
The desktop game should be simple to navigate.
The desktop game should not depend on internet access or extra services.
For the first release, the feature set should include viewing results rather than lots of extra functions.
There is no mandated technology for the first release.
The first release should be stable.
The first release should be easy to maintain.
The team may use a preferred stack if it has one.
If the save file cannot be accessed, the game shall allow the player to keep playing if possible.
If the save file cannot be accessed, the game shall clearly inform the player that progress or results may not be stored.
The game is likely to be used by multiple players on a shared home or school computer.
If the game supports multiple profiles, each player’s settings and records should remain separate.
If a puzzle is restarted, the current attempt shall stop counting and a new attempt shall begin.
When a puzzle is restarted, earlier completed results shall remain in history.
The system shall exclude obviously invalid cases from historical statistics, including cases where the save was damaged or the game never properly finished the puzzle.
Block movement shall feel responsive and predictable.
The game shall clearly count each action so the player knows what was done.
If a puzzle has a defined solution path, the game shall still allow any legal move.
The game shall not force a single exact sequence unless that is part of the puzzle design.
In a grid-based puzzle, the default block movement shall be one step at a time unless a level is designed for sliding until blocked.
If one player input legitimately causes more than one block to shift as part of a single move, the system shall count it as one action as long as it happens in one deliberate input.
Any legal sequence of correct moves shall remain valid for solving the puzzle.
Puzzle design should be fair and flexible.
The game should avoid making move order feel overly restrictive unless a specific puzzle depends on it.
The game should help the player understand that the sequence constraint is part of the puzzle and not a bug.
The game shall be usable by beginners and comfortable for adults.
The game shall provide readable text.
The game shall provide a clear, high-contrast board from the start.
The game shall support keyboard-only control.
The game shall support larger font sizing if it is easy to implement.
On the board, the keyboard shall let players move focus or the selected piece clearly.
On the board, the keyboard shall trigger valid moves without needing the mouse.
In menus, the arrow keys shall be basic expected controls.
In menus, Enter shall be a basic expected control.
In menus, Escape shall be a basic expected control.
In menus, Tab shall be used for moving between controls if needed.
No core part of the game should require the mouse.
The mouse may be available as an optional convenience.
If restoring a saved game rewinds or changes the puzzle in a way that makes the result no longer comparable, the system shall mark the attempt separately or exclude it from the main results.
The saved record shall remain honest about how the player actually completed the run.
The first release shall focus on the core puzzle experience.
The first release shall include basic progress tracking.
Hints shall be deferred to a later release unless they are found to be essential for usability.
Tutorials shall be deferred to a later release unless they are found to be essential for usability.
Account sign-in shall be deferred to a later release unless it is found to be essential for usability.
Sharing results shall be deferred to a later release unless it is found to be essential for usability.
Undo may be included in the first release as an exception.
If undo is included, the system shall clearly define whether it affects the recorded stats.
A level may have a special rule requiring the final arrangement to be held for a moment or confirmed by the player before completion is recognized.
Any special rule that delays completion recognition must be very clearly defined.
On the next launch, the system should restore the last completed save and ignore the interrupted save attempt.
The system should not let a partial write break the player's progress or leave the player in a corrupted state.
If possible, the system should fail safely and resume from the most recent valid record.
Keyboard control shall cover everything essential end to end.
The mouse may be allowed as a convenience on the board and in menus.
